sections.h: The Shepherd of Hermas: one repentance after baptism
sections.b: In Mandate 4.3 (Shepherd of Hermas 31:1-7) Hermas reports 'some teachers' who say there is no repentance except the one at baptism, 'when we went down into the water'. The Shepherd, the angel of repentance, agrees that the forgiven ought to sin no more, but announces that the Lord, knowing human weakness, has 'set a repentance' for those already called: a baptized person who falls 'has one repentance', and one who 'sins again and again and repents' will hardly live (31:6). The same 'one repentance' governs the case of an adulterous wife who returns (29:8). Lake's judgment: 'we have here the beginning of the Catholic doctrine of penance'. Codex Sinaiticus ends in the middle of 31:6, and at the key words the Athos manuscript reads 'and does not repent'; Lake follows the Latin and Ethiopic, 'and repents'.
sections.refs: Shepherd of Hermas 29:8; Shepherd of Hermas 31:1-7; Hebrews 6:4-6; Hebrews 10:26

sections.h: Clement of Alexandria and Tertullian read Hermas
sections.b: About AD 200 Clement of Alexandria retold Mandate 4.3: after baptism God gave 'a second repentance' to those who fall, but 'continual and successive repentances' are no better than unbelief (Stromata 2.13). Tertullian, a few years later and by then a Montanist, attacked the readmission of adulterers and mocked 'the scripture of the Shepherd, which alone loves adulterers' (On Modesty 10.12). Lake notes that Hermas had foreseen the charge: 'I am not giving an excuse ... I am saying it so that the one who has sinned will sin no more' (Shepherd of Hermas 29:11).
sections.refs: Shepherd of Hermas 29:11; Shepherd of Hermas 30:2; Shepherd of Hermas 31:2; Hebrews 10:26-27

claude.title: One repentance as a guard against routine
claude.body: Hermas fights two errors at once: teachers who allowed no return after baptism (Shepherd of Hermas 31:1), and the double-minded who 'are always repenting' (Shepherd of Hermas 43:4). His 'one repentance' may name the seriousness of a true return more than an arithmetic of forgiveness. This is Claude's reading; Clement of Alexandria, who also warns against repeated repentances, still keeps the count at one.
claude.refs: Shepherd of Hermas 29:8; Shepherd of Hermas 31:6; Shepherd of Hermas 43:4

sections.h: The Shepherd of Hermas: the angel of repentance
sections.b: The Shepherd who gives Hermas the twelve commandments calls himself 'the angel of repentance' (Shepherd of Hermas 25:7; 47:7; 49:1) and says, 'I am in charge of repentance ... and I give understanding to all who repent' (30:2). For Hermas repentance is itself 'great understanding': the sinner sees what he has done before the Lord, stops doing evil, does good generously, and humbles his soul (30:2). Clement of Alexandria repeated the saying. The Mandates end with an appeal to 'you who have given up on your life because of your sins' to turn to the Lord with the whole heart, with the promise that 'he will bring healing to your earlier sins' (49:2). On grief that leads to repentance, Hermas follows 2 Corinthians 7:10 but tells the believer to put grief away and put on cheerfulness (40:2-42:4).
sections.refs: Shepherd of Hermas 25:7; Shepherd of Hermas 30:2; Shepherd of Hermas 41:3-4; Shepherd of Hermas 49:1-2; 2 Corinthians 7:10

sections.h: The Shepherd of Hermas: an adulterous spouse, and remarriage after death
sections.b: Mandate 4 (Shepherd of Hermas 29:4-11) takes up a case: a believer's wife commits adultery. While her husband does not know, he does not sin; once he knows and she does not repent, he must divorce her and stay single, because if he marries again he too commits adultery. If she repents, he must take her back, 'but not over and over', since 'for God's slaves there is one repentance'. The rule holds for wife and husband alike. Lake reads the passage as a way through the clash between Jesus' ban on divorce (Mark 10:11-12; Matthew 19:9) and the rule against living with an immoral partner, and notes that the innocent party 'was not free to remarry in order to give the other the opportunity of repenting'. In 32:1-2, following 1 Corinthians 7:39-40, Hermas allows a widow or widower to marry again: 'He does not sin', though staying single gains 'more honor and great glory with the Lord'.
sections.refs: Shepherd of Hermas 29:4-11; Shepherd of Hermas 32:1-2; Matthew 19:9; Mark 10:11-12; 1 Corinthians 7:10-11; 1 Corinthians 7:39-40

sections.h: The Shepherd of Hermas: the Shepherd and the two angels
sections.b: In Vision 5 a 'glorious' man in a shepherd's dress comes to Hermas, sent 'by the most revered angel to live with you' (Shepherd of Hermas 25:2); he is the guardian Hermas was 'handed over to' (25:3) and calls himself 'the angel of repentance' (25:7). Mandate 6 teaches that two angels are with each human being, one of righteousness and one of wickedness, known by the works they stir in the heart (36:1-10). In 43:9 'the angel of the prophetic spirit' fills the true prophet in the praying church. How these angels relate to the Son of God and the Holy Spirit is one of the book's open questions (33:7).
sections.refs: Shepherd of Hermas 25:2-3; Shepherd of Hermas 33:7; Shepherd of Hermas 36:1-10; Shepherd of Hermas 43:9; Matthew 18:10; Epistle of Barnabas 18:1

common: Every believer has a guardian angel (Matthew 18:10; Shepherd of Hermas 25:3).
uncommon: Each person has both a good and an evil angel, whose works rise in the heart (Shepherd of Hermas 36:1).

sections.h: The Shepherd of Hermas: the straight road and the crooked
sections.b: Mandate 6 gives a short Two Ways of its own: faith, fear and self-control 'go two ways', toward what is righteous and toward what is unrighteous. The righteous road is straight and level; the crooked one has 'no paths, only trackless ground and many stumbling blocks' (Shepherd of Hermas 35:1-5). Hermas then sets an angel over each way inside the person (36:1-10), as the Epistle of Barnabas sets angels of light and of Satan over its two ways (Epistle of Barnabas 18:1).
sections.refs: Shepherd of Hermas 35:1-5; Shepherd of Hermas 36:1-10; Epistle of Barnabas 18:1; Didache 1:1; Matthew 7:13-14

sections.h: The Shepherd of Hermas: the Spirit as a guest in the believer
sections.b: Hermas pictures the Holy Spirit living in the believer as in a 'vessel' (Shepherd of Hermas 33:2). In a patient person the Spirit 'will live in a roomy place and will rejoice'; when bad temper comes in, 'the Holy Spirit, who is delicate, feels cramped' and tries to leave (33:3), and when many evil spirits move in, he leaves (34:5-7). Grief 'wears out the Holy Spirit' (40:2), and the believer must 'not crush the Holy Spirit who lives in you, or else he may plead with God and leave you' (41:5), an echo of Ephesians 4:30. 'The Spirit of God who was given to this flesh does not put up with grief' (41:6). In 28:1-4 'the spirit God made to live in this flesh' may be the Holy Spirit or the human spirit.
sections.refs: Shepherd of Hermas 28:1-4; Shepherd of Hermas 33:2-3; Shepherd of Hermas 34:5-7; Shepherd of Hermas 40:2; Shepherd of Hermas 41:5-6; Ephesians 4:30; 1 Thessalonians 5:19

sections.h: The Shepherd of Hermas: how to tell a true prophet
sections.b: Mandate 11 (Shepherd of Hermas 43:1-21) shows a Roman church in which prophets still spoke. The true prophet is gentle, humble and content with little; he answers no one's questions, does not speak in private, and speaks when God wills, in 'a gathering of righteous men' at prayer, when 'the angel of the prophetic spirit' fills him (43:8-9). 'Test the person who says he carries the Spirit by his works and his life' (43:16).
sections.refs: Shepherd of Hermas 43:7-10; Shepherd of Hermas 43:16; 1 John 4:1; 1 Corinthians 14:29-32; Didache 11:8

sections.h: The Shepherd of Hermas: the false prophet in the chair
sections.b: The false prophet sits in a teacher's chair before the double-minded, who come 'as to a fortune-teller' (Shepherd of Hermas 43:1-2). He gives empty answers to empty people, mixed with true words the devil supplies (43:3; Clement of Alexandria quotes this line); he seeks the seat of honor, lives in luxury, takes pay, avoids the praying church and prophesies 'in a corner' (43:12-13). In a church full of righteous people at prayer he is struck dumb (43:14). The Didache gives the same test of pay (Didache 11:12).
sections.refs: Shepherd of Hermas 43:1-4; Shepherd of Hermas 43:12-15; Didache 11:12; Matthew 7:15-20; Matthew 23:6

sections.h: The Shepherd of Hermas: double-mindedness
sections.b: Mandate 9 (Shepherd of Hermas 39:1-12) applies James 1:5-8 to a sinner who dares not pray: 'Do not reason this way ... ask him without hesitating', because God 'holds no grudge'. The double-minded 'get none of what they ask for at all'; faith 'comes from above, from the Lord, and has great power', while double-mindedness is 'an earthly spirit from the devil' (39:11). Hermas's word dipsychos is James's (James 1:8; James 4:8).
sections.refs: Shepherd of Hermas 39:1-12; James 1:5-8; James 4:8; James 3:15

sections.h: The Shepherd of Hermas: the first commandment
sections.b: 'First of all, believe that God is one. He created all things and put them in order' (Shepherd of Hermas 26:1). Irenaeus quoted these words as 'the Scripture' (Against Heresies 4.20.2), and Eusebius preserves his Greek (Church History 5.8.7). The creed echoes Deuteronomy 6:4 and James 2:19.
sections.refs: Shepherd of Hermas 26:1-2; Deuteronomy 6:4; James 2:19; 1 Corinthians 8:6

sections.h: The Shepherd of Hermas: made out of nothing
sections.b: Hermas's first commandment says God 'made all things out of what did not exist, so that they came to be', and that he 'holds all things, but he alone cannot be held' (Shepherd of Hermas 26:1). Lake's margin points to 2 Maccabees 7:28. In 47:2 the Shepherd argues from creation: God 'created the world for humankind's sake' and gave them authority over everything under heaven, so they can master the commandments too.
sections.refs: Shepherd of Hermas 26:1; Shepherd of Hermas 47:2-3; 2 Maccabees 7:28; Hebrews 11:3; Genesis 1:28; Psalm 8:6

sections.h: The Shepherd of Hermas: slander and lying
sections.b: Mandate 2 forbids slander and listening gladly to slander: the listener who believes it 'will also be guilty of the slanderer's sin'; slander is 'a restless demon, never at peace' (Shepherd of Hermas 27:2-3; compare James 4:11). Mandate 3 demands truth in every word, and Hermas weeps over a lifetime of crafty speech in business (28:1-5).
sections.refs: Shepherd of Hermas 27:2-3; Shepherd of Hermas 28:1-5; James 4:11; James 3:8; Ephesians 4:25

sections.h: The Shepherd of Hermas: love the truth
sections.b: 'Love the truth, and let only truth come out of your mouth' (Shepherd of Hermas 28:1). The liar hands back to the Lord as a liar 'a spirit that does not lie' (28:2). Hermas, who confesses he has never spoken a true word, is told that from now on truth can make even his old words believable (28:3-5).
sections.refs: Shepherd of Hermas 28:1-5; Ephesians 4:25; 2 Timothy 1:14

sections.h: The Shepherd of Hermas: give to all, simply
sections.b: 'Give to all who are in need, simply, without hesitating over whom to give to and whom not to. Give to all, for God wants his own gifts given to all' (Shepherd of Hermas 27:4). The receivers 'will give an account to God of why they received and for what'; the giver is innocent, and his giving is a 'service ... glorious in God's sight' (27:5-6). Lake notes that the Didache gives the same rule (Didache 1:5). Mandate 8 adds the works of mercy: widows, orphans, the needy, ransoming God's slaves, and not squeezing debtors (38:10).
sections.refs: Shepherd of Hermas 27:4-6; Shepherd of Hermas 38:10; Didache 1:5; Didache 4:7; Matthew 5:42

sections.h: The Shepherd of Hermas: two kinds of fear
sections.b: Mandate 7: 'Fear the Lord ... and keep his commandments' (Shepherd of Hermas 37:1, after Ecclesiastes 12:13), but do not fear the devil, who has no power over those who fear the Lord (37:2). 'If you want to do evil, fear the Lord, and you will not do it. But if you want to do good, fear the Lord, and you will do it' (37:4). In 45:4 the fear of the Lord is the believer's armor against evil desire.
sections.refs: Shepherd of Hermas 37:1-5; Shepherd of Hermas 45:4; Shepherd of Hermas 49:3; Ecclesiastes 12:13; Matthew 10:28

sections.h: The Shepherd of Hermas: the devil has no power
sections.b: The Mandates insist that the devil can test but not conquer God's slaves: 'there is no power in him' (Shepherd of Hermas 37:2); 'The devil can wrestle with them, but he cannot throw them' (48:2); he looks for partly empty jars, believers whose faith is not full (48:3-4); his threat 'is as limp as a dead man's sinews' (49:2). The Shepherd calls himself 'the angel of repentance who masters him' (47:7). Double-mindedness and evil desire are both called the devil's daughter (39:9; 45:2).
sections.refs: Shepherd of Hermas 37:2; Shepherd of Hermas 47:6-7; Shepherd of Hermas 48:2-4; Shepherd of Hermas 49:2; James 4:7

sections.h: The Shepherd of Hermas: remarriage after a death
sections.b: Asked whether a widow or widower who marries again sins, the Shepherd answers, 'He does not sin ... But if he stays by himself, he gains for himself more honor and great glory with the Lord' (Shepherd of Hermas 32:2), following 1 Corinthians 7:39-40.
sections.refs: Shepherd of Hermas 32:1-2; 1 Corinthians 7:39-40

sections.h: The Shepherd of Hermas: put on cheerfulness
sections.b: Mandate 10 makes cheerfulness a duty: 'put on cheerfulness, which always finds favor with God' (Shepherd of Hermas 42:1). The Holy Spirit was 'given to people cheerful', and the prayer of a grieving man cannot rise to God's altar, because grief mixed with prayer is like vinegar in wine (42:2-3).
sections.refs: Shepherd of Hermas 42:1-4; 2 Corinthians 9:7; Galatians 5:22

sections.h: The Shepherd of Hermas: self-control goes two ways
sections.b: Mandate 8 (Shepherd of Hermas 38:1-12) explains self-control as holding back from evil and never holding back from good: 'if you hold back from doing good, you commit a great sin'. Mandate 12 sets a good desire against evil desire, which is 'wild and hard to tame' and must be reined in (44:1-2).
sections.refs: Shepherd of Hermas 26:2; Shepherd of Hermas 38:1-12; Shepherd of Hermas 44:1-2; Galatians 5:23

sections.h: The Shepherd of Hermas: consulting a prophet like a fortune-teller
sections.b: The double-minded go to the false prophet 'as to a fortune-teller' to ask what will happen to them; 'whoever asks a false prophet about some matter is an idol worshiper' (Shepherd of Hermas 43:2-4).
sections.refs: Shepherd of Hermas 43:2-4; Acts 16:16; Deuteronomy 18:10-14

sections.h: The Shepherd of Hermas: wormwood in the honey
sections.b: 'Suppose you take a very little wormwood and pour it into a jar of honey. Is not the whole honey spoiled?' (Shepherd of Hermas 33:5). So a little bad temper spoils patience.
sections.refs: Shepherd of Hermas 33:5-6; Deuteronomy 29:18

sections.h: The Shepherd of Hermas: ransoming God's slaves
sections.b: Among the good works of Mandate 8 is 'buying God's slaves out of their troubles' (Shepherd of Hermas 38:10), in a church where Hermas himself had been sold as a slave (1:1). The book calls every believer a 'slave of God' (28:4; 29:2).
sections.refs: Shepherd of Hermas 38:10; Shepherd of Hermas 28:4; 1 Clement 55:2

sections.h: The Shepherd of Hermas: serving widows
sections.b: The first of the works that go with faith and love is 'serving widows, looking after orphans and people in need' (Shepherd of Hermas 38:10), as James 1:27 says.
sections.refs: Shepherd of Hermas 38:10; James 1:27

sections.h: The Shepherd of Hermas: business, luxury and pagan friendships
sections.b: The Mandates warn against 'showy wealth' and luxury (Shepherd of Hermas 38:3; 45:1), and say believers 'tangled up in business and wealth and friendships with Gentiles' cannot understand the things of God, like neglected vineyards overgrown with thorns (40:4-5).
sections.refs: Shepherd of Hermas 36:5; Shepherd of Hermas 40:4-5; Shepherd of Hermas 45:1; Matthew 13:22
